1.title: Governance and Risk Management
1.text: Welcome to Module eighteen: Governance and Risk Management. It covers the exam area Security Program Management and Oversight. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. five point one Explain the importance of governance, risk, and compliance artifacts. five point two Explain the impact of risk management processes on the security of the organization. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Security Program Management and Oversight (fourteen percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: Governance documents
1.text: Governance documents. The figure shows this: The governance hierarchy: policies, standards, procedures, guidelines and plans.

1.title: Governance documents, continued
1.text: Governance documents. Policies. Purpose: High-level rules set by management: what must be done and why. Binding?: Mandatory. Standards. Purpose: Specific required measures to meet a policy: baselines, passwords, physical security, encryption, R F C-based protocol standards. Binding?: Mandatory. Procedures. Purpose: Step-by-step instructions: S O Ps and runbooks. Binding?: Mandatory.

1.title: Governance documents, continued
1.text: Governance documents. Guidelines. Purpose: Recommendations: benchmarks, advisories, implementation guides, reference architecture. Binding?: Optional. Plans. Purpose: Business continuity and disaster recovery. Binding?: Operational.

1.title: Common policies
1.text: Common policies. B Y O D (bring your own device), acceptable use policy (A U P), clean desk, information security, incident response, data classification and retention, access control, data disposal, vulnerability disclosure, privacy. Exam tip: Policy equals why and what (mandatory, high level). Standard equals what exactly (specific). Procedure equals how (steps). Guideline equals advice (optional). The A U P says what users may and may not do with company resources.

1.title: Risk management process
1.text: Risk management process. Risk identification. What happens: Find risks. Items: Asset identification, stakeholder ownership. Risk assessment. What happens: Rate them. Items: Scoring, categorization. Risk analysis. What happens: Understand them. Items: Impact, likelihood or probability, owner, current mitigations, qualitative versus quantitative. Risk register. What happens: A recorded list of risks. Items: Communication, reviews. Risk treatment. What happens: Decide the response. Items: Transferring, accepting, avoiding, mitigating.

1.title: Risk management process, continued
1.text: Risk management process. The figure shows this: The four risk treatments: transfer, accept, avoid, mitigate.

1.title: Risk management process, continued
1.text: Risk management process. Transfer. Meaning: Shift the risk to a third party. Example: Cyber insurance, outsourcing. Accept. Meaning: Live with it (documented, approved). Example: Low risk, cost of fix too high. Avoid. Meaning: Stop the activity. Example: Cancel a risky project. Mitigate. Meaning: Reduce likelihood or impact. Example: Patch, add controls. Exam tip: Insurance equals transfer. Residual risk is what remains after controls. The risk owner accepts residual risk; management sets the risk appetite (how much risk is acceptable).

1.title: Business-level considerations
1.text: Business-level considerations. Business impact analysis (B I A). Finds critical functions and the effect of losing them (sets R T O and R P O). Risk appetite. How much risk the organization is willing to take. Residual risk. Risk left after treatment. Stakeholder involvement and management oversight. Decisions are owned by the business. Regulatory and legal. Laws may require specific controls.

1.title: Quantitative risk formulas
1.text: Quantitative risk formulas. S L E (single loss expectancy). Meaning: Loss from one event. Formula: Asset value times exposure factor. A R O (annualized rate of occurrence). Meaning: How often per year. Formula: Number of events per year. A L E (annualized loss expectancy). Meaning: Expected yearly loss. Formula: S L E times A R O. Example: an asset worth $one hundred thousand with fifty percent exposure has an S L E of $fifty thousand. If it happens twice a year (A R O two), the A L E is $one hundred thousand. A control costing less than the A L E reduction is worthwhile.

1.title: Quantitative risk formulas, continued
1.text: Quantitative risk formulas. The figure shows this: Worked example: S L E fifty thousand times A R O two gives A L E one hundred thousand. Exam tip: A L E equals S L E times A R O. Qualitative analysis uses ratings (high, medium, low); quantitative uses numbers and money.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors buys cyber insurance to cover ransomware losses. Which risk treatment is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Transfer. Insurance shifts financial risk to a third party, which is transfer.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A server worth eighty thousand would lose twenty-five percent of its value in one flood. What is the S L E? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: twenty thousand. S L E is the asset value times the exposure factor: eighty thousand times zero point two five equals twenty thousand.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Floods happen once every four years (A R O zero point two five) and each costs twenty thousand. What is the A L E? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: five thousand. A L E is S L E times A R O: twenty thousand times zero point two five equals five thousand per year.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Management writes a document that says all laptops must use full disk encryption. Which type of document is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A policy. A mandatory high-level rule from management is a policy, backed by standards and procedures.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. After a patch and monitoring, a small risk remains that the owner agrees to live with. What is the remaining risk called? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Residual risk. The risk left after controls is residual risk, which the risk owner may accept.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A company stops offering a service in a country because compliance is too costly. Which risk treatment is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Avoid. Ending the activity that creates the risk is avoidance.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which governance document is optional advice? Answer: A guideline. Question two. What is the difference between a standard and a procedure? Answer: A standard states specific requirements; a procedure gives the steps. Question three. Name the four risk treatments. Answer: Transfer, accept, avoid and mitigate.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is the formula for A L E? Answer: Single loss expectancy times annualized rate of occurrence. Question five. What does a risk register contain? Answer: A list of identified risks with their analysis, owners and status. Question six. What does a business impact analysis find? Answer: Critical business functions and the impact of losing them.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Documents: policy (mandatory, why), standard (specific), procedure (steps: S O P, runbook), guideline (advice), plans (B C, D R). Policies: B Y O D, A U P, clean desk, information security, incident response, classification and retention, access control, disposal, vulnerability disclosure, privacy. Risk steps: identify, assess, analyze, register, treat. Treatments: transfer (insurance), accept, avoid, mitigate; residual risk remains. Numbers: S L E equals asset value times exposure; A L E equals S L E times A R O; qualitative versus quantitative; B I A; risk appetite. In the next module, we continue the course.
